doc.title: Mike Wofford interviewed by Monk Rowe, San Diego, California, February 13, 1998

chapter: Singers: Sarah Vaughan and Ella Fitzgerald
title: What Sarah Vaughan was like to accompany
summary: She was the easiest singer to work with: professional, never complaining, giving great harmonic freedom, an excellent pianist, but repeating her sets.

story.theme_name: Singers and the musicians who accompanied them

blocks.x: The easiest singer I’ve ever worked with, of any I can think of. I mean just absolutely professional. I never heard Sarah complain once about anything, unless it was a legitimate mess-up, if a sound man or a lighting man or someone wasn’t taking care of business and doing their job, she’d be all over them, and rightfully so. But I never ever heard her complain about not feeling good, having a cold, having a sore throat, having sinus problems, and there were a lot of times when I know she didn’t feel good, traveling as hard as we did, because we traveled almost constantly. And it’s pretty remarkable because there are very few singers you could say that about. She was really unique.

Did she allow you — I don’t know if “allow” is the right word but — I assume that you did some experimenting with different chord changes and stuff from night to night, and did you ever play anything that would make her kind of look at you like — I’m not sure that works?

Not with Sarah. I have to qualify that a little bit. There was more freedom with her than with anyone I’ve ever worked with, including the biggest names down to the most kind of beginning singers that I worked with early on when I was first starting to accompany. She didn’t need any help at all. She knew exactly what she was doing. The only place you could get in trouble is she would give you so much freedom that if you got carried away and got yourself out on a limb somewhere harmonically or whatever, she would go with you. I mean she heard everything. And she would go with you into these territories, well if you weren’t prepared to follow through and didn’t have a pretty good idea of where you wanted this to end up, you could feel pretty foolish, and then at that point she might give you the ray you know. But I don’t remember that happening more than maybe a couple of times in the two years I was with her, because you couldn’t throw her. I mean it’s not like with so many pretty good singers where if you go too far they’re lost. They’re not going to be able to get it back together. That never happened with Sarah. She just was too astute. And she was an excellent pianist herself, a very good musician. She knew chords, she could sight read, she was a musician. So anyway, no, she was the easiest to accompany of anyone, because there were no predetermined parameters or rules. The one thing she did do is repeat her sets a lot. We didn’t change material very often. We would sometimes for months at a time we would perform pretty much the same show with maybe a few — you know she would give me the free reign to maybe juggle some things here and there, but for the most part we didn’t introduce a lot of new material all the time.
